parts:
Dear all,

I have two questions about my analysis (I am using the stepwise function to fit a MQM model):

1) I simulated the genotype probabilities between markers:

> sim.geno(data, step = 1, n.draws = 32, error.prob = 0.0001)
However, in my genetic map, the average marker spacing is actually more dense (0.4cM) - but there are also some bigger gaps (max = 50cM).
If I use step =1cM, there are 2 QTL reported
With step =0.5cM, I find 3 QTL (same outcome as if I consider only genotyped markers with step = 0).
Question: What distance would you recommend? Does it make sense to go below 1cM?

2) My phenotype is not normally distributed. I've read in the book, that QTL analyses are usually robust to non-normal phenotypes if significance-thresholds were calculated on genome-wide permutations but data transformation can increase power to detect QTL.
If I log2-transform the phenotype, the model fits better, explains more variance and more QTL are reported (there is one additional QTL and one of the major QTL gets broken down into two, see below):
Questions (which I hope are not too stupid):
-how do I interprete the additive and dominance effects of the QTL with a transformed phenotype? Can/should I back-transform by exponentiating?
-one major QTL turned out to be actually two QTL with different positions on the same scaffold (pos at 77cM and 132 cM). How can I tell that it's really two separate QTL and not just an artifact?

Thank you in advance for your help and answers!!!!
Anna

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] questions about sim.geno( step= ) and phenotype log2-transformation
parts:
>
> 1) I simulated the genotype probabilities between markers:
>
>> sim.geno(data, step = 1, n.draws = 32, error.prob = 0.0001)
> However, in my genetic map, the average marker spacing is actually more dense (0.4cM) - but there are also some bigger gaps (max = 50cM).
> If I use step =1cM, there are 2 QTL reported
> With step =0.5cM, I find 3 QTL (same outcome as if I consider only genotyped markers with step = 0).
> Question: What distance would you recommend? Does it make sense to go below 1cM?

If you have some really big gaps between markers, you're going to need much more than 32 imputations, and I suspect that some of the differences in results are due to imputation error. step=1 and step=0.5 should give you the same set of QTL, but with slightly more precise estimates in the latter case. step=0.5 or even small is in principle better but just more time consuming for the calculations.

You haven't said what type of cross; below I see you have 86 individuals. Sample size and density of recombination breakpoints would affect the choice of step size, as with many more individuals or which more effective recombination, you would have greater mapping precision.

> 2) My phenotype is not normally distributed. I've read in the book, that QTL analyses are usually robust to non-normal phenotypes if significance-thresholds were calculated on genome-wide permutations but data transformation can increase power to detect QTL.
> If I log2-transform the phenotype, the model fits better, explains more variance and more QTL are reported (there is one additional QTL and one of the major QTL gets broken down into two, see below):
> Questions (which I hope are not too stupid):
> -how do I interprete the additive and dominance effects of the QTL with a transformed phenotype? Can/should I back-transform by exponentiating?
You could think of the effects as being multiplicative on the original phenotype. Personally, I wouldn't try to transform back to the original scale.

> -one major QTL turned out to be actually two QTL with different positions on the same scaffold (pos at 77cM and 132 cM). How can I tell that it's really two separate QTL and not just an artifact?
>

I'd first look at how many markers site between the two QTL, and how many individuals had a recombination event between the QTL. And it seems like you're pushing the boundary of the number of parameters estimated with a sample size of 86. I'd be concerned about the evidence for those interactions.

karl

parts:
Dear Karl,

thank you very much. I really appreciate the quick answer. My cross is an F5 intercross.
I decided to stick (for now) to the un-transformed phenotype and re-ran the analysis with 1000 simulation replicates. Now, the numer (and position) of QTL is the same (3), no matter what grid size I use (0, 0.5 or 1).
To account for the non-normal distribution, I looked at the non-parametric model output of scanone and it is the same as with standard interval mapping. Also, the residuals vs. fitted plot for the MQM model looks good, so I think the phenotype isn't too bad.

Best,

Anna
